prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "GE Vernova Inc." (ticker GEV), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "GEV", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: GE Vernova Inc.
result.industry: Power generation and electrical grid equipment and services
markets: Heavy-duty and aeroderivative gas turbines and their long-term services
Steam turbines, generators and nuclear (including BWRX-300 small modular reactors via GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy)
Grid equipment: transformers (Prolec GE), switchgear, HVDC and grid automation
Grid and power software (GridOS, asset performance management)
Onshore and offshore wind turbines and services
Power conversion and battery storage solutions

mission.statement: That is our mission at GE Vernova: continuing to electrify to thrive and decarbonize the world.
mission.plain: Help the world get more electricity while cutting the pollution that comes from making it.

about.plain: GE Vernova builds the giant machines that make electricity, like gas turbines, wind turbines and nuclear reactor parts. It also makes the equipment that moves electricity from power plants to homes, such as big transformers and grid control software. After it sells a machine, it keeps earning money for decades by servicing and upgrading it. Its technology helps make about a quarter of the world's electricity.
about.customers: Electric utilities, independent power producers, governments, grid operators and big power users such as data-center companies.
about.everyday: When you switch on a light or charge your phone, there is a good chance some of that electricity was made by a GE Vernova turbine.

money.plain: gas turbines, steam turbines and decades of service on them
transformers, switchgear, HVDC links and grid software
onshore and offshore wind turbines and their upkeep
large power transformers, fully owned since 2026 (about $3.1B of 2026 sales guided)
BWRX-300 mini nuclear reactors, first one being built in Ontario

result.summary: GE Vernova has a real competitive advantage: it is one of only three makers of large gas turbines (with Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi) and owns an installed base of about 7,000 gas turbines that feeds a high-margin service business for decades. Surging power demand from data centers and electrification has sold out turbine capacity years ahead, letting it raise prices. Its wind business is a clear weak spot with ongoing losses.

pricingPower.evidence: With gas turbine backlog and slot reservations rising from 62 GW to 83 GW in Q4 2025 and to 116 GW by June 2026, GE Vernova says equipment margin in backlog rose by $8B (about 6 points) in 2025, and Power segment EBITDA margin rose to 18.8% in Q2 2026 from 16.4% while orders still grew 134% organically; Electrification book-to-bill was about 1.7.

moats.evidence: The GE name and 130+ years of power engineering give credibility with utilities; HA-class turbines hold efficiency records, but buyers decide on specs and track record rather than brand.
A turbine runs for 30+ years and is serviced mainly by its maker under long-term contracts; services were $17.1B of 2025 revenue (45%) and most of the backlog.
Selling more turbines does not make each one more valuable to other customers, apart from fleet data that improves service.
The largest installed base (about 7,000 gas turbines and 59,000 wind turbines) spreads R&D and service costs, but rivals Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi have similar scale.
Only three OEMs dominate large gas turbines worldwide; the market cannot profitably support many more, and new entrants need decades of know-how and billions in factories.
It competes with the same business model as its main rivals.
Designing and making turbine hot-section parts that survive above 1,400°C, and the 'Lean' operating system that turned Power from losses to an 18.8% EBITDA margin, are hard to copy.
Factory slots are effectively a scarce resource: it plans to reach 24 GW of gas turbine output in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030, and customers pay reservation fees to secure them.

customers.evidence: Customers keep coming back for service and capacity (Q2 2026 orders $24.2B, up 88% organically, and backlog $176B), but wind customers have suffered blade failures (e.g. Vineyard Wind 2024) and onshore wind orders fell 40% in Q2 2026.

talent.evidence: About 75,000-85,000 employees and a strong engineering heritage from GE, but no top-tier employer ranking placements found; it is not seen as a Silicon-Valley-style magnet for talent.

product.evidence: Its 7HA/9HA gas turbines are among the most efficient combined-cycle turbines and the most-ordered large turbines; it regained the No. 1 spot in advanced-frame gas turbine orders in 2024 per Turbomachinery International, while its Haliade-X offshore turbine had quality problems.

threats: Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi are expanding gas turbine factories, and Doosan is entering, which could erode pricing once the current shortage eases.
A slowdown in data-center buildouts or AI power demand could cut the order surge behind the $176B backlog.
Wind remains loss-making (Q2 2026 segment EBITDA margin -13.6%), with US policy hostile to offshore wind and past blade failures.
Execution risk on ramping gas turbine output to 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030 and on integrating Prolec GE.
Cheaper batteries, solar and reciprocating engines or on-site power could take share of new capacity from large gas turbines over time.
Tariffs and supply-chain constraints on materials such as castings, forgings and electrical steel.

ceo.name: Scott Strazik
ceo.background: Career GE executive (joined GE in 2000 via its Financial Management Program), led GE Gas Power from 2018 and GE's energy businesses from 2022; CEO of GE Vernova since its April 2024 spin-off; finance rather than engineering background.

c1.evidence: GE Vernova is a leader in power generation and grid equipment for the AI and electrification power boom, with orders up 34% organically to $59.3B in 2025 and up 88% organically in Q2 2026, though the industry itself is century-old rather than newly emerging.

c2.evidence: Utilities pick it for proven, efficient HA-class turbines, the largest installed base (about 7,000 gas turbines) and a service network that is hard to copy, an advantage reinforced by limited factory slots at only three big OEMs.

c3.evidence: Most people know the GE name, but the GE Vernova brand dates only from 2024; it is the default leader in gas turbines for professionals, not a consumer household name.

c4.evidence: It repeats its mission to 'electrify to thrive and decarbonize the world', which matters greatly over 10 years, but management is equally focused on margins, buybacks ($3.9B returned in H1 2026) and cash flow.

c6.evidence: “GE spin-off, power turbines, AI energy play”: the impression is now mostly positive thanks to the gas turbine boom, tempered by memories of GE's decline and wind turbine failures.

c7.evidence: Electricity demand is rising from data centers, electrification and reshoring, and grid investment is a multi-decade trend; its backlog grew to $176B by June 2026.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into small modular nuclear (BWRX-300 in Ontario and TVA), transformers via the 2026 Prolec GE buyout, HVDC and grid software.

m1.evidence: Strazik foresaw the gas turbine recovery and positioned for electrification, but he is a disciplined operator more than a futurist visionary.

m2.evidence: He is not a founder but has run the energy businesses since 2018 with a long-term, owner-like focus on fixing GE's power units.

m4.evidence: He emphasises 'Lean' and customer focus, but there is little public evidence of an explicitly servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: He has instilled a Lean, accountability-driven culture that lifted Power margins, though it is more an operating culture than an invention culture.

m6.evidence: He is deeply involved in operations and products but has a finance background rather than an engineering one.

m7.evidence: No controversies are known and he speaks about the energy transition, but there is no strong public record of a cause beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Scott Strazik at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Strazik is a low-key, numbers-focused executive without a celebrity public persona.

m9.evidence: He turned Gas Power around from 2018 and, as GE Vernova CEO, took operating income from -$923M in 2023 to $1,388M in 2025 and grew backlog to $176B.

m10.evidence: Lean cost discipline and cutting SG&A as a share of sales are emphasised, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: Its technology helps generate about a quarter of the world's electricity, used by billions of people.

p2.evidence: Building 500+ MW gas turbines, HVDC systems and nuclear reactors is extremely hard (only a handful of companies can) and essential for reliable electricity.

f1.evidence: Revenue fell from $33,006M in 2021 to $29,654M in 2022, then rose each year to $33,239M (2023), $34,935M (2024) and $38,068M (2025).

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 15.0% (2021) and 11.7% (2022) to 19.8% in 2025, and operating margin from -9.7% (2022) to 3.6% (2025).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had $13,120M of cash (incl. restricted) versus $2,794M of long-term borrowings and $11,957M of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from -$2,881M (2022) to $1,388M (2025) and operating cash flow from -$1,660M (2021) to $4,987M (2025).

v1.evidence: Its HA gas turbines are a top choice for efficiency and proven reliability, but Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi offer comparable machines, and its wind turbines are not best in class.

v2.evidence: No placement of GE Vernova on major best-employer rankings (e.g. Glassdoor Best Places to Work, Fortune 100 Best) was found.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, utilities worldwide would lose service on about 7,000 gas turbines and 59,000 wind turbines, threatening blackouts and stalling data-center and grid projects.
